concept.name: Self-attribution bias
concept.definition: The tendency to attribute successes to one's own skill and failures to external factors such as luck, market conditions, or other people. A self-serving attribution pattern studied since Miller and Ross (1975), it is listed among the behavioral patterns that distort investor decision-making in the SEC-commissioned Library of Congress review.
concept.intuition: Winning trades prove you are skilled; losing trades prove the market was rigged - so the mental scoreboard always flatters you.
concept.mechanics: Outcomes consistent with expectations are internalized (skill), inconsistent ones externalized (luck or manipulation), protecting self-esteem but corrupting the feedback loop needed for learning. In behavioral finance it feeds overconfidence: traders who credit wins to themselves update self-assessed skill too quickly and trade more.
concept.failure_modes: It blocks error correction: if losses are always someone else's fault, process flaws are never found. Miller and Ross cautioned that some apparently self-serving attributions reflect rational expectation-based inference rather than ego defense, complicating diagnosis.
concept.misconceptions: It is not deliberate dishonesty - the attribution pattern is largely automatic. Nor is every internal attribution of success biased; sometimes the trader genuinely was skilled, which is why contemporaneous process records are needed to tell the difference.
concept.example: After a profitable quarter a trader concludes his stock-picking is elite and doubles his size; after a losing quarter he blames manipulation and changes nothing.
